summary: Defines the role and function of IETF protocol parameter registry operators. Many protocols use commonly defined values, so registries must record assigned values and their meanings uniquely and consistently across independent implementations.

plainLanguage.summary: Many protocols need shared numbered lists so everyone means the same thing. This explains the job of the people who keep those lists.

questions: who manages ietf protocol parameter registries
what is the iana registry operator role
how are ietf protocol values assigned
subtitle: Who manages the shared number lists that keep protocols compatible.

tldr.problem: IETF protocols use commonly defined values (port numbers, error codes, options) that must be assigned consistently so independent implementations can interoperate. These assignments need to be administered by a trusted central authority.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF delegates the role of protocol parameter registry operator to a designated organization, with clear responsibilities for assignment, consistency, public access, and periodic reporting.
tldr.outcome: A single Protocol Parameter Registry Operator maintains canonical registries for IETF protocol parameters, enabling reliable interoperability while the IETF focuses on protocol design. The IETF retains authority and oversight through the IAB and IESG.
tldr.outcomeLabel: How IETF keeps values in sync

today: RFC 8722 is the current definition of the IETF protocol parameter registry operator role and remains in effect. It replaced RFC 6220 to reflect the reorganization of IETF administration under the IASA 2.0 model.

sections.title: The Need for Protocol Parameter Registries
sections.content:
Internet protocols often use commonly defined values—such as port numbers, error codes, message types, and option identifiers—that must be interpreted identically by independent implementations. For example, when one application sends data to another using TCP, both sides need to agree on what a particular port number or header field means. These values are recorded in protocol parameter registries, which serve as the single source of truth for what each value represents.

The IETF uses registries to ensure that assigned values and their meanings are uniquely defined and publicly available. This allows developers worldwide to implement standards-compliant software without ambiguity. If assignments were made randomly or inconsistently, interoperability would break.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine everyone who makes Lego building sets needs to agree on what each color block means. A master list keeps them all in sync so one person's blue block means the same thing as everyone else's.

sections.title: Organizational Structure
sections.content:
To avoid conflicts of interest and keep policy separate from allocation decisions, the IETF separates the role of protocol design from the role of managing registries. The Protocol Parameter Registry Operator—currently the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) function, operated by ICANN—handles the day-to-day assignment and maintenance of registries on behalf of the IETF.

This separation mirrors the structure used by other standards organizations like ISO, which separate standards-making bodies from registration authorities. The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) has authority to appoint and manage the Registry Operator. The IETF Engineering Steering Group (IESG) provides technical direction on what assignments are permitted for each parameter.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF makes the rules for a protocol, but they hire someone else to be the referee and keep score. The referee is impartial and just follows the rules without playing the game.

sections.title: Registry Operator Responsibilities
sections.content:
The Protocol Parameter Registry Operator has four core duties. First, it maintains registries according to policies specified in RFC documents, assigning values only as those policies direct. Second, it reviews and advises on Internet-Drafts to ensure their "IANA Considerations" sections are clear and consistent with published guidelines. Third, it operates public mailing lists for expert review processes and maintains contact information. Fourth, it reports periodically to the IAB on registry performance, including statistics on assignments and operational service levels.

All assigned values are published freely online without charge. The Registry Operator also publishes an annual report describing the status of the function. When ambiguities or disputes arise, the Registry Operator seeks technical guidance from the IESG and may request an expert be appointed to advise.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry keeper writes down who gets each number, keeps the list online for free, helps people understand the rules, and once a year tells the IETF how things are going.

sections.title: IETF Oversight and Control
sections.content:
Although the Registry Operator handles day-to-day assignments, the IETF maintains ultimate authority. The IAB defines the role, sets the terms and conditions for the Registry Operator, and appoints the organization that will perform the function. The IETF LLC (a recent administrative restructuring) identifies potential vendors and manages the contractual relationship.

The IESG is responsible for the technical direction of registries. It ensures that Internet-Drafts contain proper "IANA Considerations" sections and identifies technical experts to review complex assignment requests. The IETF Trust holds the intellectual property rights of the registries themselves, ensuring they remain under IETF stewardship for the long term.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF is like the boss who makes the big decisions: who the referee should be, what the rules are, and whether the referee is doing a good job.

sections.title: Scope and Applicability
sections.content:
This document defines the registry operator role for IETF protocol parameters as produced by the IETF Internet Standards Process. The requirements also apply generically to the extended IETF community, such as the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF). While the document typically refers to "Registry Operator" in singular form, the IETF recognizes that different operators could be selected for different protocol registries if circumstances warrant—though a single operator is preferred for consistency and economy of scale.

This RFC obsoletes RFC 6220, updating it to reflect the IETF Administrative Support Activity (IASA) 2.0 restructuring. The fundamental role and function remain unchanged, but the organizational relationships have been clarified under the new IETF governance model.
sections.plainLanguage: This explains how one person can keep all the lists, but the IETF could also hire different people for different kinds of lists if needed. A newer version of this rule reflected how the IETF itself reorganized.
